title: How to Understand the New Age of War
author: Lawrence D. Freedman
text: Podcast How to Understand the New Age of WarA Conversation With Lawrence D. Freedman Published on September 17, 2026 Play Listen to the Episode 62 minutes 00:00 / 1:02:08 0.5×1×1.5×2× MP3 Close audio player Print Print this article Save Sign in and save to read later Close Share How to Understand the New Age of War A Conversation With Lawrence D. Freedman Share in email Share on Facebook Share on X Share on LinkedIn Article link: https://www.foreignaffairs.com/podcasts/how-understand-new-age-warhttps://www.foreignaffairs.com/podcasts/how-understand-new-age-war Request reprint permissions here.Episode Details By some measures, there is more war in the world today than at any point since World War II. Today’s wars have brought a level of destruction, disruption, and global risk that would have been hard to imagine not long ago, often in places where such combat seemed a thing of the past. Policymakers once again worry about nuclear use, and military planners once again contemplate war between great powers, including the United States and China, and NATO and Russia. And all of this comes as the Trump administration dismantles key pieces of the international system and technology scrambles expectations about how wars start, unfold, and end.No one has left a greater mark on our understanding of wars past and present than Lawrence Freedman. Freedman has written a slew of definitive books on military strategy and history, and he has offered some of the most penetrating analysis of Iran, Ukraine, and more, in Foreign Affairs and elsewhere. He is emeritus professor of war studies at King’s College London.Dan Kurtz-Phelan spoke with Freedman on Monday, September 14, about the course of today’s conflicts; about what is and is not changing in the nature of war; and about why policymakers, military officers, and strategists so often start wars based on bad assumptions—and how those bad assumptions explain some of the biggest calamities in global security today.Sources:“The Age of Forever Wars” by Lawrence D. Freedman“Iran and the Forever War Trap” by Lawrence D. Freedman“The War of the Falkland Islands, 1982” by Lawrence D. Freedman“The Special Relationship, Then and Now” by Lawrence D. Freedman“Campaign 2000: Promoting the National Interest” by Condoleezza RiceThis episode of The Foreign Affairs Interview was produced by Adelaide Parker, Adrian Feinberg, Elise Burr, and Kanishk Tharoor, with audio engineering by Todd Yeager and original music by Robin Hilton. Special thanks as well to Irina Hogan.This is a rough transcript of the conversation. Please consult the underlying audio prior to citation.DAN KURTZ-PHELANLaurie, it’s wonderful to have you back on the podcast.LAWRENCE D. FREEDMANIt’s very good to be here.DAN KURTZ-PHELANThere’s no shortage of reasons why I was eager to have you back. There are plenty of wars to talk about and plenty that you’ve written in our pages in recent years that continues to shed light on all of those wars. But there is an additional reason we wanted to have you on. It’s a bittersweet one. You have been our military book reviewer for more than 20 years, and after our November/December issue, you’ll be stepping down from that post, though I hope still appearing in our pages with some frequency. I’m extremely excited about your successor, whom we will reveal soon, but we’ll still miss having you in that role.And reflecting on those decades and looking back at your work over them, my mind goes to a very big question. At the start of that period in late 2002, we were in the early years of America’s post-9/11 wars. I think that moment, if I can remember where the conversation was, Afghanistan seemed to be going pretty well, at least viewed from Western capitals, and there was debate raging about Iraq, but I think few people in that debate really registered just how consequential the mistake of that war would be.But even with those, it was, I think, hard to imagine at that time just how much major war we’d be seeing a couple of decades later and the extent to which great power war is once again something we contemplate quite seriously. Nuclear use has been talked about. The fear of that is certainly higher than it was at that point. By some measures, there’s more war in the world now than at any point since World War II. So again, to go big, how do you understand that arc? Why did we see the return of major war after a period in which it seemed a thing of the past?LAWRENCE D. FREEDMANI mean, it’s very sad, if nothing else. If you go back to the ’90s, one can overstate the optimism of that decade because there were terrible things that happened in the ’90s too, Rwanda being one obvious example. The Balkan Wars ended up okay, I guess, but they seemed difficult at times. And again, there were some terrible events during those.But by and large, the feeling was that the West was on top. It had come out ahead in the Cold War. Other countries, which had been our adversaries, were adopting Western ways. That was the meaning of globalization. And that if we were going to use military force, it would be at our discretion.And I think the first thing that 9/11 shattered was the idea that this was up to us. Somebody brought the war to the United States in a dramatic way. And it’s not that nobody had foretold that sort of event, but it seemed very worst case. And here we are when the worst case had happened.And I think that was the second impact of 9/11 is, if you said, “Well, that’s the worst case,” people say, “Well, the worst case happened.” Very fanciful scenarios were developed about how Iraq had developed the bomb, handed over to Al-Qaeda, both of which required a lot of stretch, but you didn’t dare to say that’s impossible because the impossible had happened.And I think the decisions by the Bush administration to globalize the war on terror, to make it not about how you deal with this wretched Al-Qaeda stuck somewhere in Afghanistan, but you’d make it a much bigger thing, you’d try and sort out all sorts of old scores and issues that hadn’t been done before, that’s what got us into trouble. If it had been confined to Al-Qaeda and Afghanistan, I think the outcomes would’ve been very different, including in Afghanistan, but ambition took over and then hubris as well.DAN KURTZ-PHELANIf we turn to the war that is consuming the Middle East right now and a lot of American foreign policy attention, the one in Iran, you’ve been pretty unsparing about the extent of the Trump administration’s error in both going to war and conducting it. You’ve called it a stupid war, which is much worse than a bad war. It does, however, seem in keeping with some of the persistent American errors when it comes to the use of force, especially in that region. Do you see it as different in kind or just in degree of error? And to the extent it is similar to those, why does the US keep making this kind of mistake?LAWRENCE D. FREEDMANI mean, it is a stupid war because the consequences were forecast. Anybody who dealt with the Middle East, who looked at the Iran issue really since the Bush administration knew the two things that would happen would be the Strait of Hormuz and Hezbollah come back again. So there was no surprise there.You can argue, of course, that the Americans are not unique in making the sort of error that assumes that because you’ve got your really great power and you’ve got super military forces, that you can do what you want, and that as long as you get it over quickly, all will be well. So Trump in that sense made the same error as Putin, and obviously this is not yet, in terms of human life, death, and destruction, as bad a war as Ukraine, but it’s very consequential.And I think what to me still is what’s staggering about it is the lack of thought that went into it. I mean, to have Benjamin Netanyahu come along with a plan and then discuss that and decide, “Oh, it seems a good idea.” I mean, even with Iraq, I mean, there was a year of active debate and discussion, and it was based on false premises, and they still got it wrong, but at least everybody knew what the issues were and where the risks were, and some attempt was made to mitigate them, but at least there was an active public debate.This one just got everybody by surprise. There was no full discussion even within the administration. And of course, you’ve got an administration that’s been hollowed out, that doesn’t have the capacity and expertise that previous administrations have. So this is the same old mistake of underestimating the enemy, believing that you can get it all sorted out quickly before all the bad things could happen. These are pretty standard mistakes. Again, not just for the United States, other countries have made them as well, but the legacy of this is going to be with us for many years, even assuming we can get through the immediate economic consequences, which are pretty serious.DAN KURTZ-PHELANYou wrote a fantastic piece for Foreign Affairs, I believe last year, called “The Age of Forever Wars,” where you talked about the short-war fallacy, the way that this kind of assumption that decisive, overwhelming force will bring a quick victory. You wrote a follow-up recently called [“Iran and the Forever War Trap”] where you show how this thinking is part of the error that led us to this point. What’s the mindset that makes that such a frequent mistake by both American policymakers but also others?LAWRENCE D. FREEDMANI think the problem is that’s what military planners plan for. I mean, nobody in their right mind plans to launch a long war. If you’re going to go to war, you want it over quickly, and you assume that’s true of your adversary as well. So the mindset of military planners is quite short-term.And indeed, if you try to think about how to prepare for a protracted war, our societies would find it very difficult because you’d need far greater mobilization, more stocks, it would consume a lot more resources. Whereas the hope is always with a short war, you get it over quick and you barely notice it, it’s barely a blip in terms of the economy and industrial capacity and so on. And you look at Russia and you see how Russia has had to transform its economy for the worse because of its failure with its short war.So the problem is that military planners don’t think about this, that they’re focused on short war. They get excited by the latest technology, and you can see that again with this one, particularly with the targeting and sort of the speed with which you get from and identifying targets to actually destroying them, the role of AI and all of that.And I think there was also a mindset, which very strong in this Pentagon, which is, you look at military force in terms of military objectives, you don’t look at in terms of the wider political objectives. And so it took a long time before Pete Hegseth seemed to recognize this was not a victory, even though in terms of the loss of capability, Iran appeared to have come off worse, boasting when the ceasefire was announced, so this is a victory with a capital V and so on. Looks downright embarrassing now. So I think if you are going to fight a war, you need to link them with what you’re trying to achieve politically.And I think the problem with Iran is the political objectives were muddled. It started with regime change, then it was getting a better nuclear deal. Now it’s opening the Strait of Hormuz, but there was never clarity on this. I mean, I think the regime change in particular was very problematic.I mean, the Israelis seem to have convinced themselves, as they do with a number of their adversaries, that if you take out sufficient numbers of the elite, if you decapitate, effectively they’ll fall apart, but they don’t, not these countries. They thought about it, and Iran was well aware of what might be coming up. I mean, Trump seemed to have had in mind that if you took out the right people and left better people, that you could do a Venezuela-type deal with them, which was complete fantasy.And you could have got a better nuclear deal by negotiating. So you’ve got no nuclear deal at all at the moment and an Iranian regime that has been reminded of why it might want nuclear weapons.So for all these reasons, it was ill-thought-through, objective poorly defined, and a military system geared to the short term and taking out the enemy’s military system rather than trying to work out what’s necessary to do to get to what we want to achieve.DAN KURTZ-PHELANHas anything in Iran’s military response particularly struck you? Have you been impressed in an immoral sense by their use of drones or the way they’ve escalated or anything else?LAWRENCE D. FREEDMANI think from Iran’s point of view, it was always going to be about survival. Once it was clear that the Americans were not going to use ground forces, their task became a lot easier. So the issue is one of survival, which meant having replacements for senior people in case they got killed, which many did, being prepared to suppress any popular protests. Well, it’d already shown that they were prepared to slaughter their own people in the thousands, so they were well-prepared for that. Protecting as much as possible of your missile production as well as launching capability, and they’ve been able to do that.And then I think what surprised people was the speed with which they went for the Strait of Hormuz, because in June ’25, they’d had a much more cautious response. The Americans had concluded that the Iranians probably wouldn’t fight very hard. The Iranians concluded that they needed to, so they were prepared. And I think once that happened, we were in a completely different conflict for which there was no shortage of warning. It shouldn’t have come as a surprise, but there wasn’t great preparation.DAN KURTZ-PHELANThere’s a line in your “Age of Forever Wars” essay: you write, “When a short-war plan does not produce the anticipated victory, the challenge for military leaders is to achieve a new alignment between means and ends.” How would you do that in Iran at this point from a US perspective?LAWRENCE D. FREEDMANI think it’s very difficult because unfortunately, I don’t think this is great for the Iranians. The hardliners have used the opportunity to take control. And if you were concerned about the plight of the Iranian people, they’d be interested in compromises. I mean, they can take income from the Strait of Hormuz if they get that sorted out at some point, but what they really need is Iranian assets to be unfrozen and for essentially the oil industry to be allowed to flourish.Now, all of that was made possible by the MoU. So there was a deal available, which was not a bad deal from the Iranian perspective, but I think they got fixated on the Strait of Hormuz as their leverage. And instead of taking the opportunity to let that open and then really... I mean, they’ve shown that they can close it at any time. So they weren’t going to lose their leverage just by letting it open and allowing more negotiations to take place on the nuclear side and frozen assets and so on.Now we’ve got a real problem because you depend on debates within Tehran, of which we have very little influence or control, in which the hardliners certainly have the advantage. And we’ve used up a lot of our capacity. I mean, the United States can occasionally knock things out and hit tankers going to Iranian ports, but it can’t make a material difference to Iranian capabilities at the moment. So you’re relying on economic pressure, which is real, and you would wish the regime took it into account, but the regime has got other priorities.In my mind, but maybe this is too influenced by what happened with the hostage crisis in 1980, they’re waiting until after the midterms, and then they’ll see. I think they want to hurt Trump. He was part of the assassination of their comrades and mutilated the current Ayatollah and killed his father, maybe an Israeli bombs, but the Americans are part of it. I think they want to punish.DAN KURTZ-PHELANJust as they wanted to hurt Jimmy Carter and wait until-LAWRENCE D. FREEDMANSo famously, the hostages were only released as Reagan was inaugurated.DAN KURTZ-PHELANIn going back and reading all of the excellent work you’ve done for Foreign Affairs over the years, I was struck by a line in a piece you wrote in 2006. This was after you’d done the UK’s Official History of the Falklands War. And in reflecting on European or British views of the American approach, the use of force, you wrote, “The problem with Washington since World War II has been not so much its predilection for using military force as a first resort as its hesitation and uncertainty when going to war.” Is that the kind of flip side of the short-war fallacy, that it’s kind of lack of commitment to a serious war because of that delusion, or is there some other dynamic intention with that?LAWRENCE D. FREEDMANIt is a problem. It seems to be either one thing or the other, but not very nuanced in between.I mean, if you look back to, again, going back to the 1990s and the factors that influenced Blair as British Prime Minister after 9/11, Blair was very worried that the Americans were drifting away. I mean, a lot of the issues that we now worry about in terms of in Europe about the American commitment to our security and so on were all present then.And if you look at the famous article that Condoleezza Rice wrote for you during the 2000 campaign, clearly there was no great interest in humanitarian intervention at all, which he thought it was not how the United States should comport itself of what Colin Powell had said. So the idea that Blair was seized on, that Western countries had to take a far greater responsibility for making the world generally a better place, and that may include using military force.I mean, that was why when 9/11 came, he thought this was the moment when he needed to persuade Bush that there were ways of doing this that would be more widely beneficial. So it comes back to the old line about allies fears of either abandonment or entrapment. Either the US ignores your problems and needs you to sort them out even though you struggle to do so, or it gets so involved that you get caught up with things that actually increase the danger rather than ease them, the challenge of being a junior partner in an alliance.DAN KURTZ-PHELANYou pointed out the ways in which Putin going into Ukraine was similarly subject to the short-war fallacy or the delusion. You’ve more recently described the situation in Ukraine as a “hurting stalemate,” which means each side is trying to increase the pain and cost to the other side and then hope that that affects decision-making. It’s not clear that Putin has done the kind of recalibration you recommend for leaders when the short-war fallacy comes back to bite them.Looking at the war now, it does seem like each side is trying to increase costs, especially to populations back at home, and hoping that affects decision-making. I think on the Ukrainian side, there’s been more solidary and commitment than certainly most of us would’ve imagined five years ago before the war started. Whether that can sustain through what will presumably be a very tough winter for Ukrainians is a separate question. But on the Russian side, this ultimately comes down to Putin and his own sense of his own interests and potential threats to his rule.What are you looking for here? What is your theory of how this might proceed if you’re trying to be optimistic from a Ukrainian perspective? And is that the kind of best theory of victory that we can come up with for the Ukrainians at this point?LAWRENCE D. FREEDMANI mean, the term hurting stalemate is not mine, but the basic idea that it’s not clear how either side wins in the way it wants to win and they’re both hurting in the process, that’s true.So I think one of the first things I wrote on the full-scale invasion, for my Substack, not for you, was I said this is a war Putin can’t win because I just couldn’t see how he could occupy and subjugate all of Ukraine. And that remains the case. And it’s still the case that even if he achieved the immediate military objectives, you have to wonder what sort of prize the Donbas is now. It’s been ruined by the war, by the aggression. But Putin believes somehow that this is a thing that he has to win because failure to do so will undermine the credibility of him as a leader, there will be an awful lot of explaining to do as to what this was all about, why the economy has been brought down for really rather limited territorial gains. And so he’s been very stubborn.And again, go back to the first thing I wrote, it was thinking about the difference between a democratic society and an authoritarian one. I mean, at least still in our countries when we screw up, we can talk about it and urge our governments to find a way out or throw them out if they fail to do so. That’s not possible in Russia.Moreover, you’ve got a system which, as far as we can tell, does not provide the leader with the truth. Now, he may know that his forces are not doing as well as claimed. He should have cottoned on by now that he’s been forecasting imminent victory for a couple of years now and may wonder why it hasn’t yet happened, but he doesn’t let on.And this causes Russian forces at the front some difficulties. And we’ve seen recently in Lyman and so on, some real setbacks for Russian forces over egg it, but it’s not trivial. So we’re left with a question which we’ve had since the start: what is it that will persuade Putin that he should cut his losses and cut a deal? And so far, he just hasn’t been prepared to do so despite the degradation of the Russian economy and so on.I think, at the moment, the general view—it’s a Ukrainian view, and I think probably a Russian view—is that we’re into another six-month period. Can the Ukrainians cope with the winter? Can the Ukrainians find more money to fund their war basically from Europe? Because as things stand, Russia has been pretty systematic about degrading the Ukrainian economy as Ukraine has done its best to degrade the Russian economy.Will he still be far away or unable to take the fortress cities? And if that’s the case, is somebody going to be able to say in the Kremlin, “We’ve really got to stop this. If we can’t succeed when the condition seems so propitious and with the Ukrainians strengthening their hand with new ballistic missiles starting to come on stream and so on, they’ve shown real imagination, originality in tactics and technologies and so on. Really, it’s time to get out”?I mean, the American mediation efforts are pretty amateurish, so I don’t think... But they’re there if Putin wants them. I mean, I think that’s, again, the Ukrainian view. It’s not that they are that interested in American proposals. They just want to see if there’s any concessions coming through, at which point I think they would quite like a ceasefire.But it has to be said, and we must keep this in mind, even if you wanted a ceasefire and you weren’t trying to solve all the different issues between Russia and Ukraine, a ceasefire would be a tremendously difficult thing to actually negotiate. Where is the front line? Both sides have different views about where it is, who’s going to decide. Russians go around planting flags, and then the people who’ve planted the flags get killed, but the image has been taken. So they make claims about holding places that they don’t hold.So I don’t think a ceasefire would be very easy, or at least it wouldn’t get beyond a cessation of fire, but it wouldn’t get into marking the line of contact. I think it’s just going to be tremendously difficult. And then the Russians will want economic sanctions eased and so on. So even if you don’t want a big peace negotiation, which could take a year, even just getting a ceasefire agreement in place could be really difficult.And the Americans can’t deliver it by themselves. As soon as you start talking about sanctions, you’ve got to talk to the EU and the UK and Canada and so on. And given the tortured nature of relationships between the US and its allies, that’s not going to be easy either.DAN KURTZ-PHELANAre there historical parallels that are illuminating here of a personalist leader like Putin who seems almost suicidally dogged and unshakeable until he’s not? The examples that jump most immediately to mind suggest otherwise, that you end up in a self-destructive kind of delusional spiral, but maybe there’s something that points in the other direction?LAWRENCE D. FREEDMANWell, I mean, you’re talking about individual psychologies here. I mean, the obvious one is Hitler, who eventually shot himself in his bunker, but we’re not going to get to that stage with Russia because Ukraine isn’t going to invade and march to Moscow. I think everything needs to be looked at in its own terms. And I think one of the things this does, these wars do, both the Americans and the Russians, is there should be a reminder to IR theorists that you can have all the historical models that you like; in the end, when you’ve got these types of individuals in leadership positions, predictability becomes very difficult.DAN KURTZ-PHELANIt’s challenging in a moment when so many of the major powers are led by individuals who are similarly personalistic in their approach.LAWRENCE D. FREEDMANWell, it’s just a lot of individuals, isn’t it? I mean, we don’t talk about countries; we talk about Putin and Trump and Erdogan and Netanyahu and Xi and so on.Now, there’s always some restraints. They’ve all got to, in some ways, be sensitive to their wider political and economic situations. But people despise the great man theory of history, and these aren’t particularly great men, but they’re all men, and they’re all very powerful.DAN KURTZ-PHELANHow have you understood the conversation around Russian nuclear use in Ukraine as you’ve heard the fears expressed by policymakers? It’s obviously hard to know exactly what intelligence they’re seeing, but do you see that as a kind of plausible fear or something that Putin is doing to spook Western supporters of Ukraine?LAWRENCE D. FREEDMANI’d be more sanguine on that than many other analysts. And I think the reason is because I think the nuclear arsenal is very important to Putin. I mean, it’s what makes Russia a great power because without it, it would be a very large and rather unsuccessful middling power. And without the nuclear capability, NATO probably would’ve come in and supported Ukraine. There would’ve been no massive risks in not doing so. So it’s had a deterrent effect, which we shouldn’t ignore. And Putin has always concentrated in his own commentary on the importance of NATO not sending its own troops, not fighting side by side with the Ukrainians.A lot of the other stuff has come from Medvedev and some media characters and analysts like Karaganov, who basically think that they haven’t used their nuclear arsenal enough, or Medvedev’s case, as long as you talk about Armageddon, that maybe you can stop the alliance sending particular weapons or agreeing new targeting rules or Finland and Sweden can join the alliance. And it’s just overused. I mean, there’s so many threats which were never followed through that it’s just lost to all credibility, which I think was the complaint by some of the hardliners in Russia.So my view is that probably even if NATO forces did end up on Ukrainian soil, as they may do after a ceasefire, I still think Putin would be reluctant to start a nuclear war. I mean, it’s not a great idea. It’s not obvious what you gain from it.People tend to assume that it panics... Well, I think it probably would panic the Ukrainians. It would panic people in Moscow too. I mean, it wouldn’t go down well in Beijing. So I don’t particularly think it’s high on Putin’s to-do list, but it does have a deterrent effect to major intervention. Beyond that, there’s plenty of ways, as Putin has shown, of escalating this war without having to use nukes.So there was this period in September, October ’22, and we’ll maybe at some point find out more about Russian decision-making. But what my view was then is that we shouldn’t allow ourselves to get spooked.And the sad thing is that a lot of things that might have been done for Ukraine early on were not done because of some view that there were red lines that would be crossed. And Putin was never going to go to war because you’ve got to send tanks, not just anti-tank missiles. We got ourselves, I think, taking it far too seriously, as if his finger was hovering over the button all the time.DAN KURTZ-PHELANAs we’ve taken that threat quite seriously, it’s striking how little reaction there’s been to steps that Putin has taken in Europe that get grouped into this category of hybrid war, but that would’ve been quite unthinkable without a major NATO response a few years ago, but he has been quite willing to take risks and escalate in that sense.LAWRENCE D. FREEDMANYeah, and it’s a worry, and I think Europeans are trying to get the measure of this problem because how do you respond to all of this stuff? I mean, if you have Russian agents going around Europe doing stuff, as they have been doing, some of it quite dangerous, using explosives or cyber attacks or drone incursions or whatever, do you respond in kind, which is difficult and potentially provocative? Maybe we do respond on cyber stuff and you and I don’t know about it.But then what are the messages you’re trying to send? Well, this is all about, is it because Europe supports Ukraine and then he’s trying to stop Europe supporting Ukraine? So the best answer is to keep supporting Ukraine. And that’s the most straightforward thing to do. And obviously, he’s got in mind that we may have a different Europe quite soon with different governments in France, potentially in Germany eventually, even the UK.Well, again, I think it also adds to the urgency from a European point of view of helping Ukraine as strongly as possible now because the longer this thing goes on, the harder it becomes for everybody and the greater the hurt.DAN KURTZ-PHELANDo you foresee changes in the role or prominence of nuclear weapons in global security in the years ahead? I think there have been two different arguments that are in tension, if not in direct opposition. One is that deterrence seems to be less solid than we might’ve thought, given Ukrainian attacks on the Russian homeland and attacks on Israel despite its having nuclear weapons. There was a pretty significant war between two nuclear powers in India and Pakistan not long ago. On the other hand, watching Iran and watching the North Korean experience by contrast, you can imagine there are lots of other smaller countries that have an interest in getting their own nuclear arsenals now. What do you think that will mean in terms of the role of nuclear weapons?LAWRENCE D. FREEDMANI mean, it seems to me there’s two things that are going on at the moment. First, all in all, deterrence works. NATO has not joined in the war on Ukraine’s side. It has given Ukraine a lot of support, but it hasn’t actually joined in. Equally, Russia, it’s getting closer. It’s not attacked NATO territory. They have a perfectly good argument otherwise for interdiction of supplies going into Ukraine hasn’t done that. Nuclear weapons haven’t been used, which is not unimportant.In India and Pakistan, we’ve had a number of fights now which have been contained. I think they get harder each time, but so far, they’ve been contained. And I think it’s because the leadership groups on both sides are aware that, at some point, it could become hard to contain. Once the restraints are off, then you’re getting into very uncharted territory.So I don’t buy the view that nuclear weapons and deterrents have not affected international behavior. I think they have in quite important ways. It’s just if you have exaggerated views about the effects, then you can say you’re disappointed.I think we think every time something bad happens, it’s a failure of deterrence, even when there are things we didn’t try to deter. So I think we have to be very careful about how we talk about it.I don’t think there’s anything that’s happened that is going to persuade existing nuclear powers not to carry on being nuclear powers and to talk about nuclear deterrence as the best guarantor of their security.The other thing that’s going on is what happens to countries that are not nuclear powers. Now obviously, you can hear Ukrainians talk about the Budapest Memorandum of 1994 and wonder what would’ve happened if they’d stayed in the nuclear game. You have a lot of countries wondering whether the guarantees from the United States, which always had small print, but the small print seems rather large at the moment, can rely on them.And this works out differently in the Indo-Pacific region to how it does in Europe. In Europe, you’ve got the UK and France trying to work out how they can talk about their nuclear capabilities in such a way as to reinforce wider European security.But for Japan and South Korea and so on, it’s a more difficult problem. So you may have more nuclear powers. I mean, that’s always been the simple assumption that if alliance reassurances don’t reassure and extended deterrence loses its credibility, then the natural next step is to look to your own potential nuclear capabilities. It wouldn’t take Japan or South Korea that long to become nuclear weapons.All you can see in the Gulf now, one of the consequences of the Iran war is the US doesn’t turn out to be a very helpful ally. It created a war in which its allies in the region get hurt and hasn’t done an awful lot to come to their aid. We’ve seen with the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.So I don’t know whether Donald Trump at some point will want to just cut all alliance ties, but it doesn’t really matter. I mean, the idea anyway was always there that threatening to go to nuclear war on behalf of other countries was a bit unnatural. And that argument is now being reinforced.In Europe, it’s an issue, but in the end, the Europeans should be able to increasingly take over more of their own security, given that Russia may be in an aggressive mood, but it’s also weakened itself over the long term anyway. It’s probably a similar line that could be said about military analysts watching technological changes in war.As you’ve watched these wars, are you struck by changes in the basic nature of warfare as we’re seeing it now? FREEDMANYeah, it’s a broken record really on this. No, I think the problem for students with military power is you’re always going to look at the next big thing and fixate on it and assume that it can be transformational, like people are doing with AI at the moment.
